title: Penrose Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Penrose wells have a 140 ft median depth; local drilling and finished-well costs depend on fractured mountain bedrock.
h1: Penrose, Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost
intro_html:
Buying land around Penrose means evaluating the well as part of the property, not as an afterthought. Records within 5 miles show 864 permitted wells, though only 509 are recorded as constructed and 170 report a pump yield.

The local ground is fractured mountain bedrock, and nearby records include Florence, Williamsburg, Rockvale, Brookside, Lincoln Park, and Cañon City. That setting can produce useful household wells, but results vary from one parcel to the next. The most reliable starting point is to review nearby well depths, reported yields, permits, and the proposed septic and building layout before committing to a purchase.

sections.heading: Penrose well depths vary with the mountain rock
sections.html:
Penrose wells with reported depths have a median of 140 feet. The middle half runs from 66 to 285 feet, which is the range a driller is most likely to use when developing an initial bid. Still, the spread is wide: 34% of recorded wells are under 100 feet, 42% fall between 100 and 300 feet, 16% between 300 and 600 feet, and 8% exceed 600 feet.

The deepest reported well reaches 2,180 feet. Most permits identify an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer; 840 wells are in that category, compared with 10 Dakota wells and 5 Dakota Group Aquifer wells. In fractured granite and gneiss, fractures control both depth and water supply, so a nearby shallow well does not guarantee the same result on your lot.

sections.heading: What a Penrose well may produce
sections.html:
Among the 170 wells that report a pump yield, the median is 10.0 gallons per minute. The middle half produces 5.6 to 15.0 gallons per minute. That is generally a workable range for a household when the well, pressure system, storage, and fixtures are designed together.

Yield records show 1% under 1 gallon per minute, 14% from 1 to 5 gallons per minute, 52% from 5 to 15 gallons per minute, and 34% above 15 gallons per minute. The 1% under 1 gallon per minute is not a reason to ignore low-yield risk. Ask for the well completion report and pumping information, then have the proposed home and irrigation demand evaluated separately. A permit does not promise a particular yield.

sections.heading: Penrose water levels are documented only sparsely
sections.html:
Only 19 permitted wells near Penrose report a static water level, so the local water-level picture is limited. Those records show a median depth to water of 48 feet, with the middle half between 20 and 144 feet.

That small sample does not establish a reliable decade-by-decade decline or prove that the water table is stable. Static water level also changes with location, season, pumping, and the time since a well was used. For a property under consideration, request the actual well report and ask whether the measurement was taken before or after pumping. A driller can also explain how the expected water level affects pump setting, trenching, pressure equipment, and the cost of bringing water into the house.

sections.heading: Who has drilled around Penrose, and when
sections.html:
Permit activity is not limited to one period. Records show 5 permits from the 1950s, 17 from the 1960s, 73 from the 1970s, 185 from the 1980s, 124 from the 1990s, 120 from the 2000s, 77 from the 2010s, and 18 from the 2020s. The newest permit year in the records is 2026. Older wells may still serve homes, but their construction, pump, and water-quality documentation deserves careful review.

The most active drillers in the records are Finney & Son (Finney, Leonard), with 187 wells; Finney Drilling (Finney, Larry D.), with 60; and Arkansas Valley Drilling (Moore, Todd A.), with 53. These records identify past permit activity, not a recommendation or a guarantee of current availability. Confirm licensing, scheduling, and the scope of any current bid directly.

sections.heading: A Penrose well budget starts with depth
sections.html:
Penrose drilling is priced in fractured mountain bedrock, described in the local cost model as granite and gneiss. The typical drilling rate is $65 to $100 per foot. At the 140-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $9,100 to $14,000.

That is not the complete water-system price. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $15,100 to $26,000 at the median depth. A deeper-than-median hole, difficult access, extra casing or grout, longer trenching, and electrical work can move the final bid higher. Use the depth range of 66 to 285 feet as a planning range, not a promise. Ask each driller what is included and what happens if the hole is dry or must be deepened.

sections.heading: Checks that matter before building near Penrose
sections.html:
Low yield and dry-hole risk are the first technical concerns in fractured bedrock. Review neighboring well reports, but do not treat one successful well as proof for another parcel. A well producing less than 1 gallon per minute appears in 1% of the yield records, and only 170 wells report any pump yield.

Water quality also needs testing. Within about 10 miles, the map includes 26 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 48 historic mine features, and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site. Those mapped sites do not prove contamination at your property, but they support testing before purchase and again before occupancy. Locate the well, septic system, replacement area, driveway, and house together. Confirm the permit conditions with Colorado DWR, and remember that domestic use, stock use, irrigation, and additional water needs may require different approvals or an augmentation plan in an over-appropriated basin.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Penrose, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth near Penrose is 140 feet. The middle half runs from 66 to 285 feet. About 34% are under 100 feet, while 8% exceed 600 feet. The deepest recorded well is 2,180 feet, so a nearby well is useful for planning but cannot guarantee the depth on a particular parcel.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Penrose?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $65 to $100 per foot in fractured granite and gneiss. At the 140-foot median depth, the drilled hole is about $9,100 to $14,000. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is about $15,100 to $26,000. Deeper drilling and difficult access can increase the bid.

faq.q: How much water do Penrose wells produce?
faq.a: Among 170 wells with reported pump yields, the median is 10.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 5.6 to 15.0 gallons per minute. Records show 1% under 1 gallon per minute and 34% above 15 gallons per minute. Have the proposed home’s demand checked against the actual well report.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Penrose?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from a permit or a neighboring well. There are 26 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 48 historic mine features, and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site within about 10 miles. Test the property’s water before purchase or occupancy, with testing selected for local conditions and the well’s location.

faq.q: Are Penrose wells getting deeper or running dry?
faq.a: The records do not provide enough static water-level measurements to establish a trend: only 19 wells report a static water level. Those show a median depth to water of 48 feet, with the middle half from 20 to 144 feet. Fractured bedrock can vary sharply between parcels, so review nearby reports and obtain a site-specific driller’s assessment.
